passages.happening:
‘After a long time, in the third year of the drought’ (verse 1), the LORD sends Elijah to Ahab with word that he will send rain. The famine is severe in Samaria (verse 2). Ahab calls Obadiah, who is over his palace. Obadiah fears the LORD greatly; when Jezebel killed the prophets of the LORD, he hid a hundred of them, fifty to a cave, and kept them in food and water (verses 3-4). The king and Obadiah split up to search the land for grass to keep the horses and mules alive (verses 5-6).

Elijah meets Obadiah on the road and tells him to go and tell Ahab that he is here. Obadiah is afraid. Ahab has searched every nation for Elijah, and if the Spirit of the LORD carries Elijah away, Ahab will kill the messenger (verses 9-14). Elijah swears, “As surely as the LORD of Hosts lives, before whom I stand, I will present myself to Ahab today” (verse 15), and Obadiah goes to tell the king (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
The drought announced in 17:1 has lasted long enough for the question to become unbearable: who truly gives the rain, Baal or the LORD? The king's own worry, in this scene, is his horses.

Jezebel's killing of the LORD's prophets is not told anywhere else. It shows that the promotion of Baal under the house of Omri meant persecution, not only toleration. Obadiah, a senior official at the court, shows that faithful worshipers of the LORD survived even there. He is a different man from the prophet whose short book bears the same name.

His fear is understandable. To announce Elijah and then have him vanish would cost the messenger his life. Elijah's oath ties his word to the LORD of Hosts, before whom he stands, as he did when he first spoke to Ahab.
passages.later: In Acts, after the baptism on the desert road, ‘the Spirit of the Lord carried Philip away’ (Acts 8:39), as Obadiah feared the Spirit would carry Elijah away (verse 12).
passages.asks: Obadiah served a wicked king's household and quietly saved a hundred lives. Ask what faithful work you can do inside a place you did not choose. And ask what fear keeps you from carrying a message you have been given.

passages.t: The troubler of Israel, and a god who did not answer
passages.happening:
When Ahab sees Elijah, he says, “Is that you, O troubler of Israel?” (verse 17). Elijah answers, “I have not troubled Israel” (verse 18). It is Ahab and his father's house who have, he says, for they have forsaken the LORD's commands and followed the Baals. He tells Ahab to gather all Israel to Mount Carmel, with the four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal and the four hundred prophets of Asherah who eat at Jezebel's table (verse 19).

Then Elijah comes before all the people: “How long will you waver between two opinions? If the LORD is God, follow Him. But if Baal is God, follow him” (verse 21). The people do not answer a word. Elijah sets the terms. Each side will prepare a bull on wood without lighting it, and each will call on its god: ‘The God who answers by fire, He is God’ (verse 24). The people agree.

The prophets of Baal call on Baal from morning until noon, ‘But there was no sound, and no one answered as they leaped around the altar they had made’ (verse 26). At noon Elijah mocks them: perhaps their god is lost in thought, or busy, or away, or asleep and must be woken (verse 27). They shout louder and, as was their custom, harm their own bodies (verse 28). They rave until the time of the evening sacrifice, ‘But there was no response; no one answered, no one paid attention’ (verse 29).
passages.hearers:
Ahab calls Elijah the troubler of Israel, and Elijah throws the word back. It is the word used of Achan, the man whose sin brought disaster on all Israel. The real troubler is the one who breaks faith with God.

Mount Carmel is a ridge running from the coast inland, near the border between Israel and Phoenicia. Its heights catch the rain clouds off the sea and were known for their green growth, a natural place for a contest over rain, and it may already have held shrines for more than one god.

Elijah's question uses a verb that means to limp or hobble: how long will you go limping between two opinions? The same verb describes the prophets' dance around Baal's altar. Most of Israel did not mean to give up the LORD. They meant to keep him and add Baal, as one more hedge against a dry year. Elijah says that cannot be done.

Baal was the storm god, pictured with a thunderbolt, so a test to be answered by fire, by lightning, put him on what his worshipers thought was his own ground. His prophets used practices known from ancient religion: a hopping dance around the altar, and wounding themselves to rouse their god's attention and pity. Israel's law forbade it. Elijah's mockery plays on the myths themselves, in which gods travel, sleep and are busy elsewhere.

The key word of the contest is answer. The people do not answer; Baal does not answer; no one answers.
passages.later: Joshua had said to Achan, ‘Why have you brought this trouble upon us?’ (Joshua 7:25), with the same word. The law said, “You must not make any cuts in your bodies for the dead or put tattoo marks on yourselves. I am the LORD” (Leviticus 19:28).
passages.hard:
Why does Elijah mock the prophets of Baal, and what should be said of their wounding themselves?

Elijah's mockery is aimed at a god, not at the people's pain. It exposes Baal as no god at all: the one who was said to travel, sleep and wake is simply not there.

The self-wounding was part of their worship, and Israel's law forbade it. In the Bible's picture, a child of the living God does not have to win heaven's attention with pain. The text records the practice in a few words, and these notes do not dwell on it.

If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today: a doctor, a pastor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line in your country. If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Israel kept the LORD and added Baal, and Elijah called it limping. Ask what you have added beside God as a hedge against a dry year. And ask what answer you are waiting for from something that cannot answer.

passages.t: Fire from the LORD, and the Kishon
passages.happening:
Elijah calls the people near and repairs the LORD's altar that had been torn down. He takes twelve stones, one for each tribe of the sons of Jacob, builds the altar, and digs a trench around it (verses 30-32). He has the offering and the wood soaked with water three times, until the water fills the trench (verses 33-35).

At the time of the evening sacrifice he prays: “Answer me, O LORD! Answer me, so that this people will know that You, the LORD, are God, and that You have turned their hearts back again” (verse 37). “Then the fire of the LORD fell and consumed the sacrifice, the wood, the stones, and the dust, and it licked up the water in the trench” (verse 38). The people fall on their faces: “The LORD, He is God! The LORD, He is God!” (verse 39).

Elijah orders the prophets of Baal seized, and not one is to escape. He brings them down to the Kishon Valley and kills them there (verse 40).
passages.hearers:
The time of the evening sacrifice was a fixed moment of daily worship at the temple in Jerusalem, and Elijah times his prayer to it. His twelve stones recall the twelve tribes. Though the kingdom was divided, Elijah treats Israel as still one people under the covenant God made with Jacob. Pouring water on the altar in a drought was a startling act of confidence.

His prayer is short, and it asks for God's glory and the people's return: that they will know that the LORD is God, and that he has turned their hearts back. The fire is meant to bring Israel home, not only to win an argument. The people's cry, The LORD, He is God, is Elijah's own name turned into a confession.

The Kishon Valley lies below Carmel's northern side.
passages.later: Malachi promised that God would send Elijah again, and ‘he will turn the hearts of the fathers to their children’ (Malachi 4:6). Luke says that John the Baptist would go before the Lord ‘in the spirit and power of Elijah’ (Luke 1:17), and Jesus said of John, ‘he is the Elijah who was to come’ (Matthew 11:14).
passages.hard:
How should a reader understand Elijah's killing of the prophets of Baal (verse 40)?

This is a violent scene, and readers rightly feel its weight. The text tells it in one verse, and these notes do not dwell on it. In its setting, Elijah was applying the law of Deuteronomy 13 and 18:20, which treated a prophet who led Israel to other gods as guilty of a capital crime against the covenant, like treason against the nation's true king. These prophets also served a royal campaign that had already killed the LORD's prophets (verses 4, 13).

Christians broadly agree that these were laws for Israel as a nation under God's direct rule, at one moment in its story. The church was never given the sword. The New Testament meets false teaching with teaching, with discipline inside its own fellowship and with prayer, and it leaves final judgment to God. When James and John wanted to call down fire from heaven on a Samaritan village that would not receive Jesus, “Jesus turned and rebuked them” (Luke 9:55).

So it must be said plainly. This chapter gives no one today a warrant to harm, threaten or silence anyone over religion: not a person of another faith, not a person who has left the faith, not a family member. When Christians have used passages like this to justify persecution, they sinned against the Lord they claimed to serve.
passages.asks: Elijah prayed that God would turn the people's hearts back. Ask whether you want people to come home to God, or only to be proved wrong. And ask whether your zeal for God has ever made you harder toward people than he is.

passages.t: A cloud like a man's hand
passages.happening:
Elijah tells Ahab, “Go up, eat and drink, for there is the sound of a heavy rain” (verse 41). Ahab goes up to eat and drink, ‘But Elijah climbed to the summit of Carmel, bent down on the ground, and put his face between his knees’ (verse 42).

He sends his servant to look toward the sea. There is nothing. Seven times Elijah sends him back (verse 43). The seventh time the servant says, “There is a cloud as small as a man’s hand rising from the sea” (verse 44). Elijah sends word to Ahab to harness his chariot before the rain stops him. ‘Meanwhile, the sky grew dark with clouds and wind, and a heavy rain began to fall’ (verse 45). Ahab rides to Jezreel, and the hand of the LORD comes on Elijah, who tucks his cloak into his belt and runs ahead of the king all the way (verse 46).
passages.hearers:
The drought ends as it began, with Elijah's word, and now with his prayer. The prayer for rain is persistent, repeated seven times, and the answer starts small: a cloud the size of a hand.

Jezreel, where Ahab had a royal residence, lay about 17 miles, or roughly 27 kilometers, east across the plain. Elijah running ahead of the king's chariot is a picture of the LORD's power on his prophet.

The day ends in victory, but not in a changed kingdom. The next chapter shows that one day of fire did not turn Jezebel or reform the court, and that the prophet himself was left exhausted. Carmel settles who is God. It does not settle whether Israel will follow him.
passages.later: James points to this prayer: ‘Again he prayed, and the heavens gave rain, and the earth yielded its crops’ (James 5:18). He calls Elijah ‘a man just like us’ (James 5:17).
passages.asks: Elijah prayed seven times and the answer came as a cloud the size of a hand. Ask what you have stopped praying for because nothing came the first time. And ask whether you would notice a small beginning of God's answer.
